sources.title: Human History Map imported summaries
sources.note: The current Wikipedia-derived paragraph stretches Hadramawt across several modern governorates and into Dhofar; this packet replaces that overly broad framing.

sources.title: Human History Map 1000 borders
sources.note: Exact 45-position Polygon includes tested Hadramawt, Mahra and Dhofar points while Qana belongs to the separate Yemen layer.

sources.title: Human History Map 1279 borders
sources.note: Exact 59-position expanded Polygon takes Qana and extends into southern Oman.

sources.title: Human History Map 1492 borders
sources.note: Exact 69-position Polygon reaches about 59.84 east and 22.28 north, far beyond a strict Hadramawt core.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 borders
sources.note: Retains the huge 69-position southern-Arabian Polygon for the 1500 to 1530 interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 1530 borders
sources.note: Exact Polygon abruptly contracts to 21 positions and a Hadramawt core; Mahra, Dhofar and Oman-interior points move to Mahra, Gharra or Oman layers.

sources.title: Human History Map 1700 borders
sources.note: Preserves the contracted 21-position target through its last exact interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 1715 borders
sources.note: The exact id disappears, but audited Mukalla, Shibam, Tarim, Sayun and al-Shihr points have no automatic replacement owner.

sources.title: Ḥaḍramawt, Encyclopaedia of Islam
sources.note: Scholarly regional reference distinguishes the strict Wadi Hadramawt sense from broader geographical uses.

sources.title: Water sharing, territory and society in Yemen’s lowlands
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis explains that ancient Hadramawt was centered on Shabwa and that the familiar broad geographic sense emerges in medieval Arabic texts.

sources.title: Archaeological Sites of the Kingdom of Hadramout in Shabwah
sources.note: Yemen’s UNESCO submission dates the ancient kingdom to roughly 1020 BCE to 225/230 CE and describes Shabwa, Qana and its inscriptions and archaeology.

sources.title: The Sāda in History: a critical essay on Ḥaḍramī historiography
sources.note: Cambridge study stresses scarce medieval documentation and genealogical or clan agendas in accounts of law, Sufism and institutions.

sources.title: Hadramut
sources.note: TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi outlines local Rashidi, Ayyubid, Rasulid, Tahirid and Kathiri phases and town-level political plurality.

sources.title: Writing the Ethnic Origins of the Rasulids in Late Medieval South Arabia
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study shows how Rasulid chroniclers reshaped a South Arabian origin story to bolster dynastic legitimacy.

sources.title: L’Arabie marchande: state and commerce under the Rasulid sultans
sources.note: Research-institute book record frames Hadramawt as one region within a larger Rasulid sultanate and documents state, commerce and source criticism.

sources.title: The sixth/twelfth century in Oman and Hadramawt
sources.note: Oxford history describes fragmentary twelfth-century evidence, the end of Ibadi political power in Hadramawt and changing Indian Ocean trade.

sources.title: Old Walled City of Shibam
sources.note: UNESCO documents sixteenth-century tower houses, older mosque and castle elements, rival-family defense, spate-irrigated fields and vulnerable earthen construction.

sources.title: World Heritage Papers 7: Shibam’s waste-reuse system
sources.note: UNESCO paper explains vertical waste shafts, liquid/solid separation, fertilizer reuse and the relationship between sanitation, gardens, mud and town form.

sources.title: Haid Al-Jazil and Wadi Daw’an
sources.note: Yemen’s UNESCO submission describes long-used agriculture, water management, honey, herding, mud, straw, palm and sidr construction, with later continuity caveats.

sources.title: Tarim City, Hadramout
sources.note: Yemen’s UNESCO submission documents Tarim’s religious learning, mud construction, water installations, walls and fifteenth-century origin of al-Mihdar Mosque.

sources.title: Historic City of Al-Mukalla
sources.note: Yemen’s UNESCO submission records an early-eleventh-century port, Rasulid fortification in 1271 and the separate al-Kassadi emirate beginning in 1703.

sources.title: Say’un Palace
sources.note: Yemen’s UNESCO submission dates the palace before the sixteenth century, records Badr Abu Tuwayriq’s 1519 residence and describes ventilation, drainage and earthen craft.

sources.title: Sharma: a medieval commercial entrepôt on the Hadramawt coast
sources.note: Excavation monograph dates the fortified warehouse port about 980 to 1180 and documents six phases plus Indian Ocean imports from China to East Africa.

sources.title: Al-Shihr, gateway of Hadramawt on the Indian Ocean
sources.note: Excavation and textual study covers seventh to sixteenth-century al-Shihr, including fish, incense, ambergris, camels, Indian pottery and limited tell sampling.

sources.title: Hayrij, Sharwayn and Halfat: ancient ports of Mahra
sources.note: A 174-site survey identifies several ninth to twelfth-century ports and distinguishes Mahra coastal history from Hadramawt’s Sharma and al-Shihr.

sources.title: French archaeological survey in Wadi Hadramawt
sources.note: Field survey describes irrigated fields, palms, sandy areas, settlement by water and the danger of floods requiring dikes, banks and canals.

sources.title: Hydrology, ideology and irrigation in ancient Southwest Arabia
sources.note: Geomatics and ethnoarchaeology in Wadi Sana link runoff, water rights, territory and social relations while warning against purely environmental explanations.

sources.title: Rivers of the Hadramawt watershed during the Holocene
sources.note: Geoarchaeological study reconstructs an arid late-Holocene watershed where rainfall intensity, aquifers and sediment shaped river behavior and settlement.

sources.title: The Islamic Port of al-Balīd between land and sea
sources.note: Archaeology and history identify distinct Dhofar dynasties, Rasulid rule from 1279 and later Kathiri involvement, showing why Dhofar cannot simply equal Hadramawt.

sources.title: Landscape History of Hadramawt
sources.note: University of California archaeological report explains survey methods, long landscape histories and the risk of projecting ancient kingdoms or timeless desert stereotypes onto later people.

sources.title: Some irrigation systems in Hadramawt
sources.note: Historical study records water systems and flood evidence, including a destructive 1348 flood near Tarim that damaged palms and mosques.

sources.title: UNESCO mission report on Shibam and Wadi Do’an
sources.note: UNESCO mission describes flood-diversion walls, palms, beekeeping, sheep and camel herding, hill towns and mudbrick buildings as a living landscape.

sources.title: Spate irrigation in Yemen
sources.note: FAO technical reference explains diversion of episodic floodwater, sediment and community maintenance; used only to clarify the mechanics of a long-lived system.

sources.title: Medieval agricultural texts from Rasulid Yemen
sources.note: Scholarly project catalogs Rasulid almanacs, treatises and tax records on crops, seasons and irrigation while distinguishing Yemen-wide texts from local proof.

sources.title: Food supply and court redistribution in Rasulid Yemen
sources.note: Research repository record shows elite food allotments, including for royal women and enslaved people, and connects redistribution with port trade.

sources.title: Kitab al-Safar: a Rasulid guide to managing travel
sources.note: Columbia edition presents a fourteenth-century Yemeni ruler’s advice on weather, fatigue, illness, hunger, thirst, foods and medicinal plants.

sources.title: Ulema, Medicine, and Community in Yemen’s Long Fifteenth Century
sources.note: Oxford study centers Baḥraq al-Hadrami’s didactic Galenic medicine and explains care, scholarly health texts and the danger of assuming doctors were always present.

sources.title: Arabic manuscript collections in the Democratic Republic of Yemen
sources.note: Scholarly survey records Tarim and Mukalla manuscript holdings, including local historical and medical works, while noting catalog and dating problems.

sources.title: Research on Hadramawt documents
sources.note: University of Halle project describes surviving local legal and administrative archives, with the Kathiri collection beginning in 1622.

sources.title: Power, legitimacy and sovereignty in Hadramawt
sources.note: Cambridge repository thesis locates Abdallah al-Haddad, 1634 to 1720, at Hawi beside Tarim and identifies his Book of Assistance as a lasting teaching text.

sources.title: Abdullah b. Alevi el-Haddad: his life, works and Sufi thought
sources.note: Ankara Yildirim Beyazit University hosts Büşra Betül Punar’s 2019 thesis; section 7.2 dates Risalat al-Muawanah to 1069 AH, or 1658 to 59 CE.

sources.title: Risalat al-muawanah library catalogue record
sources.note: Japanese academic union catalogue supplies the Arabic title, scholarly transliteration, authorship and Arabic-language bibliographic identity.

sources.title: Islamic Intellectual History in the Seventeenth Century: references
sources.note: Cambridge bibliography independently attributes and romanizes Abdallah al-Haddad’s Risalat al-Muawanah.

sources.title: The Hadrami Network
sources.note: Historical study traces merchants, scholars, revenue collection and movement around Tarim, Aden, Dhofar and the Indian Ocean without assuming one diaspora class.

sources.title: A History of Modern Yemen sample chapter
sources.note: Cambridge sample distinguishes Shafi‘i Hadramawt, local religious mediation and brief wider Yemeni claims from uniform day-to-day political control.

sources.title: Studies in Global Slavery: medieval Yemen
sources.note: Open Brill monograph documents enslaved soldiers, concubines, cooks, quarry laborers and officials in medieval Yemen while stressing scattered evidence and different lives.

sources.title: The Portuguese off the South Arabian Coast: review
sources.note: University of Chicago journal record verifies the scholarly edition of Hadrami chronicles used to study Portuguese activity on the coast.

sources.title: Cambridge history excerpt on Portuguese Indian Ocean expansion
sources.note: Cambridge excerpt uses Hadrami chronicles and places coastal violence and trade disruption inside wider sixteenth-century Indian Ocean competition.

sources.title: On the Edge of Empire: Hadhramawt, Emigration, and the Indian Ocean
sources.note: SUNY Press historical ethnography, used explicitly as later comparison for households, oral history, gender, education and social hierarchy rather than direct medieval proof.

proposedOverrides.summary: A carefully bounded guide to the changing ports, towns, rulers, families, farming, scholarship, medicine and sanitation hidden under the atlas’s shifting “Hadramaut” state layer from 1000 to 1715.
